en: Preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Pointing to the Palm of the Hand):

Prajñā is without cognition; all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent. Their root source is the wondrous essence of the one true reality (*ekasatya*), while their manifestations are the floating names of the two truths (*dvayasatya*).
These appear to be real yet are like illusions; they cannot be characterized as either real or unreal. They are neither separate nor joined, yet neither separate nor joined.
That which can be clarified is the reason why emptiness is not empty and existence is not existent; they mutually establish one another without hindrance and may simultaneously negate one another.

They may both exist and both vanish; their disappearance and establishment are without obstruction, and their concealment and manifestation are sovereign. This is called the sublime essence of Prajñā.
Alas, how regrettable that the ordinary mind is easily deluded and the fire of wisdom is difficult to kindle—like attempting to catch the wind with a net, it is as if one were following after...
To grasp at the moon upon the waves is to undergo toil in vain, which instead becomes an obstacle;

thus, the entanglement of a hundred sufferings and the convergence of a thousand calamities all stem from this single thought of attachment. This *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is concise in its text yet rich in meaning;
its words are manifest, yet its principles are profoundly abstruse. It first opens the two gates of emptiness and form, specifically to shatter the dual attachments to existence and non-existence.
When existence and non-existence are exhausted, the true mark (*dharmatā*) can be revealed; when form and emptiness are unified, the wondrous meaning finally becomes complete.

If one understands this daily application, one has already mastered more than half of the path of Prajñāpāramitā. I have observed that among the various commentaries by past masters, few have reached its profound depths.

Only the two commentators Xianshou and Gushan truly [penetrated it]. As for the elder generals of the Dharma-arena, they merely gathered extensively from the sūtras and śāstras to elaborately spread the "traps" (*śūnyatā-yoga*).

Since this is not something that can be mastered by beginners, I have specifically provided these "pointing-at-the-palms" instructions so that they may be easily seen, thereby facilitating the study of beginners.
However, as a journey of ten thousand li begins with a single step, may those who observe this take no heed of it.
In the year of Jiawu, on the first day of autumn, the day of the Buddha’s Joy,
the Bhikṣu Yuánxián of Gǔshān monastery bows his head in prostration and offers this preface and eulogy.
This old man has now reached eighty years of age; he has gathered up all worldly affairs.
Yet this shadow of his pervades every direction—its exposure is so manifold that no amount of concealment can suffice.
Do you understand?
Within the body with marks, the markless body is seen clearly and distinctly only when one bows the head.
This was the self-inscription by the Elder Yongjue on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*— Pointing to the Palm.
Composed by the Dharma-transmitting śramaṇa Yuánxián of Gǔshān.

Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra. "Prajñā" is here translated as "wisdom," which refers to the spiritual awakening to profound mysteries and the subtle resonance with the true source. "Pāramitā" [is here translated as "perfection"].
"Much" (bahu) here refers to "reaching the other shore" (pāramitā); that is, by means of this wondrous wisdom, one turns back from the faults of saṃsāra and reaches the limit of true emptiness.
Prajñā is the essence (tattva), while pāramitā is the function (upāya). Only when essence and function are united does the name [Prajñāpāramitā] arise;
this is to distinguish it from a wisdom that has not reached the other shore. "Mind" (citta) is a metaphor, used to illustrate that this sūtra is...

The essential core of the six hundred fascicles of this great collection is like a human being: although one possesses five organs and a hundred skeletal members, the mind is that which presides over them.
The first six characters represent the Dharma that is explained (*saṃdeśya-dharma*), while the subsequent character "jīng" (經) represents the teaching that explains it (*saṃdeśaka-śāsana*).
"Jīng" is primarily defined as "constant," and it is also defined as "path. This indicates that the Dharma explained herein is the path of the Sages.

The universal norm inherent in all beings and the constant Way that remains unchanged through antiquity and the present is precisely the essential path for transcending the mundane and entering the sacred.
When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty.
It delivers one from all suffering and distress.
This is a brief indication of the essential framework based on practice.

As for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, because this Bodhisattva’s wondrous wisdom perfectly illuminates emptiness and understands that there is nothing to obstruct, he is thus able to have and to not have, and to empty and to not empty.
Because one can attain great mastery over form (*rūpa*), one receives this name. A "Bodhisattva" is a transliteration of the Sanskrit *bodhisattva*;
in the language of China, it means "one who awakens sentient beings. The term "Bodhisattva" is used by abbreviation.

One who practices profound *prajñā* refers to the *prajñā* being cultivated, which is the emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), wherein there is only the single true mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*), and is not like the partial [emptiness] of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

That which is observed superficially is the illumination that "the five aggregates are all empty," meaning one has attained the vision that the self-nature of the five aggregates is fundamentally empty;
this is the principle of the two kinds of emptiness, seen by profound wisdom. The five aggregates are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Form refers to the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and half of the mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); it does not refer merely to the illusory body. Sensation refers to the illusion...
The body experiences external objects and attains their utilization, distinguished by suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

*Saṃjñā* (perception) refers to the mind taking external objects as its conditions and forming mental images (*nimitta*). *Saṃskāra* (volitional formations) refers to the activity of conditioning, arising and ceasing moment by moment in an unceasing flux.
*Vijñāna* (consciousness) refers to the discrimination of preceding objects. Consciousness is the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*), while sensation (*vedanā*)...

Perception and volition are both deluded minds that arise in conjunction with the mind; "crossing over all suffering and distress" means that upon realizing and seeing true emptiness, such afflictions are exhausted, and one shall attain liberation from the two kinds of birth and death—those of the segmented and those of transformation.
Originally, ordinary people grasp at the five aggregates as "self" and "mine," and from this, [delusion] arises.
Deluded, they create karma and transmigrate through the six realms, willingly enduring all manner of suffering with no prospect of escape.
Although those of the Two Vehicles do not cling to these as "self" or "mine," they still grasp at the aggregates (*skandhas*) as being substantially real.

Consequently, they become addicted to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, viewing the triple world as a prison and failing to give rise to the vow to deliver sentient beings; this is called being a scorched sprout or a rotten seed, destined for no realization.
Out of profound compassion for them, the Buddha expounded this Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā so that they might realize the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty;
thus, their bodies and minds become like illusions and the world becomes like a transformation, whereby the two attachments are forever extinguished and the three obstacles are suddenly eliminated.
They may then long ride upon the white ox, broadly transporting all sentient beings together to the other shore, where the Buddha and sentient beings [are non-dual].
The names of both cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
From this point downward, up to the attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, all [teachings] extensively set forth the true meaning according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Śāriputra, among the Buddha’s disciples, was foremost in wisdom; as he manifested as a śrāvaka to serve as the leader of the assembly, the Buddha called him by name and addressed him, saying:
"That which I call 'perceiving that the five aggregates are all empty' is not [as it might seem]."

The emptiness that is apart from the aggregates is precisely the emptiness that is within the aggregates. In your own school, you merely know that there is no person within the aggregates, yet you do not realize that the aggregates themselves are also not real.
To insist that one must extinguish form (*rūpa*) before emptiness can be seen is to grasp at the emptiness of annihilation.
You should understand that form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; they must not be viewed as distinct. For...
Emptiness and form are fundamentally one entity; form is the form of emptiness and has never been non-empty, and thus is not different from emptiness.
Emptiness is the emptiness of form and has never been non-form, and thus is not different from form.

How could one grasp emptiness apart from form, or seek to see emptiness by extinguishing form? Furthermore, fearing that people might still maintain the dualistic view of emptiness and form, the Buddha said:
He further told them: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; the two truths eternally coexist, and the single flavor is constantly manifest.
It is neither one nor two, yet it is both one and two. Engaging with existence, one is not entangled by existence; contemplating emptiness, one is not intoxicated by emptiness.
The unimpeded harmony of arising and ceasing, the non-reliance on any fixed point—this is where the profound purport of Prajñā is fully contained."
Although feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not material substances possessing physical obstruction, they are all equally illusory;

their nature as empty reality is no different from that of form. Therefore it is said, "they are likewise so. This is the essential meaning of Prajñā, and students should apply themselves to it with all their heart.
Question: The old commentaries employ the analogy of water and ice, which has been widely followed by many; why is this not the case here?
It is unnecessary to answer this, for their principles and metaphors are not comparable.
Although emptiness and form possess a relationship of mutual establishment, one does not manifest emptiness by destroying form, nor does one manifest form by destroying emptiness.
When water freezes into ice, the characteristic of water is destroyed; when ice melts into water, the characteristic of ice is destroyed. Thus, the destruction of one manifests the other.
Because they do not understand at all the meaning of the emptiness of form, it is not employed here.
Śāriputra, the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas is that they are neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

"These dharmas" refers to the aforementioned five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "The mark of emptiness" is the manifestation of the principle of the two kinds of emptiness—the emptiness of the five aggregates. For where there are dharmas, there is arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease; now that these dharmas have vanished, there remains only the single true void. How could there be anything further to speak of regarding arising and ceasing and so forth? There was an ancient who composed [this verse]: [Verse omitted per instructions] ...therefore it is called "the emptiness of all dharmas. This is what is meant by "the emptiness of all dharmas. Furthermore, as for "all dharmas," they refer to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). "The mark of emptiness" means that the six sense bases are themselves empty; this is the principle of the emptiness of persons and phenomena. Because there are dharmas, there is arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease. Now that these dharmas have perished, there is only the single true void. How could there be anything further to speak of regarding arising and ceasing and so forth? Therefore, it is said: "The emptiness of all dharmas is itself empty. This is what is meant by "the emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas. Furthermore, as for "all dharmas," they refer to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). "The mark of emptiness" means that the eighteen elements are themselves empty; this is the principle of the emptiness of persons and phenomena. Because there are dharmas, there is arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease. Now that these dharmas have perished, there is only the single true void. How could there be anything further to speak of regarding arising and ceasing and so forth? Therefore, it is said: "The emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas is itself empty. This is what is meant by "the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas. Furthermore, as for "all dharmas," they refer to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). "The mark of emptiness" means that the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves empty; this is the principle of the emptiness of persons and phenomena. Because there are dharmas, there is arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease. Now that these dharmas have perished, there is only the single true void. How could there be anything further to speak of regarding arising and ceasing and so forth? Therefore, it is said: "The emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas is itself empty. This is what is meant by "the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas. Furthermore, as for "all dharmas," they refer to the four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). "The mark of emptiness" means that the four noble truths are themselves empty; this is the principle of the emptiness of persons and phenomena. Because there are dharmas, there is arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease. Now that these dharmas have perished, there is only the single true void. How could there be anything further to speak of regarding arising and ceasing and so forth? Therefore, it is said: "The emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas is itself empty. This is what is meant by "the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of all dharmas. Furthermore, as for "all dharmas," they refer to the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*). "The mark of emptiness" means that the three gates of liberation are themselves empty; this is the principle of the emptiness of persons and phenomena. Because there are dharmas, there is arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease. Now that these dharmas have perished, there is only the single true void. How could there be anything further to speak of regarding arising and ceasing and so forth? Regarding the interpretation of "before the Way," "during the Way," and "after the Way" as referring to the manifestation of the characteristics of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), this is not my own view.
If even "Buddha" is not established when the characteristics of true emptiness are manifested, how much less so could there be "before the Way," "during the Way," or "after the Way"?

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the empty characteristic of all dharmas," some masters interpret it as the "real characteristic of true emptiness. Out of respect for the Sūtra, which clearly states that these [dharmas]... I do not dare to follow such interpretations.

How can the mark of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas) be altered into a mark of reality? One might think that once all delusions have been eliminated, there is no need for anything "not true," and thus conclude that the mark of emptiness is itself the mark of reality.
This is not so; for illusory form and true emptiness both take the mark of reality as their essence.
If one awakens to this mark of reality, it is not only true emptiness that is the mark of reality, but illusory form as well.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says: "This Dharma abides in its station; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
If one now merely identifies the characteristic of emptiness as the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), then is it not biased in claiming it to be the true characteristic?

Furthermore, although the characteristic of emptiness is indeed the true characteristic, within the true characteristic the word "emptiness" cannot be attached. It would be better simply to rely on the scriptural text as authoritative.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; and no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no consciousness-element.

"Within emptiness" refers to the emptiness of all dharmas mentioned above. Because the characteristic of true emptiness manifests and the myriad dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, they are all non-existent;
this does not mean that the nature of dharmas is destroyed, for they are fundamentally non-existent. The following passages may be understood accordingly.

The five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements are all comprised within the two categories of form and mind; they differ only in how they are expanded or condensed according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to no old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death.
This clarifies that within true emptiness there are no twelve links of dependent origination. These twelve are fundamentally what the Pratyekabuddhas contemplate.

The stages are as follows: first, ignorance (*avidyā*), which refers to the state of being deluded regarding the nature of awakening; second, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), which refers to the performance of karmic actions.
These two links constitute the causes produced in the past. Third, consciousness (*vijñāna*), which refers to the arising of deluded thoughts at the initial moment of entering the mother’s womb.
Fourth, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which refers to the gradual development of various physical and mental characteristics within the womb. Fifth...

The sixth link, *ṣaḍāyatana* (the six sense bases), refers to the formation of the six faculties within the womb. The seventh, *sparśa* (contact), refers to the engagement of the six faculties with the six objects after birth.
The eighth, *vedanā* (feeling), refers to the experiencing of worldly phenomena such as the pleasant and the unpleasant;
these five links constitute the results experienced in the present life. The ninth, *tṛṣṇā* (craving), refers to the arising of greedy attachment toward worldly things.
Ninth is grasping (*upādāna*), which refers to the arising of a mind of attachment toward various objects.
Tenth is becoming (*bhava*), which refers to creating the causes of outflow (*āsrava*) that can summon future results. These three links constitute the causes produced in the present life.
Eleventh is birth (*jāti*), which refers to receiving a body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the future. Twelfth is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which refers to—
The future body undergoes old age and death; these two links are the fruits to be experienced in a future life.

These twelve links encompass the causes and effects of the three periods of time; their arising one from another in mutual dependence is called the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti-mukha*), and their ceasing one from another in mutual dependence is called the gate of cessation (*nivṛtti-mukha*). Within true emptiness, all of these are entirely absent. How could there be birth and death?
It is also because existence is fundamentally non-existent.
There is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path;
this clarifies that within true emptiness there are no Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths are originally the objects of contemplation for the Śrāvakas.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) is the world’s manifold sufferings, which are the fruit of the world; Accumulation (*samudaya*) is the performance of various karmas, which is the cause of the world;
Cessation (*nirodha*) is *nirvāṇa*, which is the supramundane fruit; and the Path (*mārga*) is the Eightfold Noble Path, which is the supramundane cause.
Within true emptiness, none of these exist at all, because their nature is fundamentally non-existent.
"There is neither ignorance nor attainment.
This clarifies that within true emptiness, not only are the aforementioned phenomena absent, but the wisdom that realizes emptiness is likewise unattainable;
and not only is the wisdom capable of realizing emptiness unattainable, but the principle of emptiness that is known is also unattainable.

To reach this state, both medicine and illness vanish, and both mind and its objects are extinguished; there remains only the single true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). This is the ultimate achievement of Prajñā. Question:
Previously, form and emptiness were established as a dual pair; why now is everything said to be non-existent? Answer:

What was previously established was established in such a way that it never failed to be exhaustive. What is now non-existent is non-existent in such a way that it never fails to [reveal]... [the ultimate].
When it is said that there is existence, this refers merely to the presence of its marks, while its nature is fundamentally non-existent;

when it is said that there is non-existence, this refers merely to the fact that its nature is originally non-existent, while its marks are not destroyed. Thus, while existing, it is correctly extinguished; while vanishing, it is eternally established.
Such is the essential principle of Prajñā.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no mental hindrance;
because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; being far removed from perverted thoughts and delusions, he attains ultimate Nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[He] said: "From this point downward, by means of the statement that 'nothing is attained,' it is revealed that there *is* attainment. Relying on this light of non-attainment, one realizes that both mind and objects are empty;
every point of contact is transparently clear, and one is liberated without obstruction. Since there is no obstruction..."
Thus, wherever one turns, there will be no obstacles of the suffering and calamities of birth and death; therefore, there is no fear.
Not only is there no fear, but even the delusions and inverted dreams since beginningless time can be distanced.
These inverted dreams and delusions are precisely ignorance and affliction (*kleśa*). Once afflictions are absent, one can ultimately reach *nirvāṇa*.

The ground of Nirvana—here translated as "Perfect Quiescence" (yuánjì)—is called "perfect" because it possesses all virtues without exception, and "quiescent" because all hindrances are exhausted without exception;
this refers to the cause being able to bring the fruit to completion. It is not only Bodhisattvas who rely on this to attain Nirvana;
even the Buddhas of the three periods of time follow no other path, but realize the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] solely by relying upon this.
Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Nirvāṇa are the fruit of cessation for a Buddha; Perfect Enlightenment is the fruit of wisdom for a Buddha.

Now, when a Bodhisattva speaks of "Nirvāṇa" and a Buddha speaks of "Perfect Enlightenment," these are instances where the Buddha’s words are mutually abbreviated in meaning, yet both must necessarily be fully present.
Question: Previously it was stated that there is "nothing to be attained," yet now it is stated that there is "something to be attained. Why is this? Answer: This...
There is something to be attained, yet it is simply the attainment of non-attainment; there is nothing else to be attained.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
It is able to eliminate all suffering because it is true and not false. Thus, one speaks of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Mantra of Prajñāpāramitā is as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
The former is the explicit teaching of Prajñāpāramitā, while the latter is the esoteric teaching of Prajñāpāramitā; thus it is both explicitly taught and esoterically taught.
This is because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ, and thus their entry [into the path] varies.

Furthermore, the explicit teaching is for generating wisdom to extinguish the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the esoteric teaching is for causing one to recite and uphold [the mantra] to generate merit and extinguish sinful karmic hindrances (*karmāvaraṇa*).

These two teachings are given so that, by extinguishing these two hindrances, one may accomplish the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*). Now, as I am about to explain the secret mantra, I shall first praise it.

As for its function, it is intended to encourage practitioners so that they may joyfully uphold it and thereby attain swift efficacy. Because it can destroy demonic obstacles, it is called the "Great Divine Mantra";
because it can destroy the darkness of ignorance, it is called the "Great Illuminating Mantra"; because it can reveal the ultimate principle, it is called the "Unsurpassed Mantra";
because it can equalize the supreme fruit, it is called the "Mantra Equal to the Unequaled. The Buddha is not equal to ordinary beings; [this mantra] makes one equal to him.
Therefore, it is called "unequaled" (*asama*); yet, because it is able to be equal to all Buddhas, the word "equal" (*sama*) is repeated.

"Able to eliminate all suffering" refers to the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and all forms of suffering. Regarding the phrase "now the mantra is revealed": since the actual words of the mantra were not previously disclosed, they are revealed here.
This cannot be explained through ordinary reasoning, for it is the secret language of the Buddha and is not within the scope of those on the stage of causes (*hetu-bhūmi*).
You should simply believe, accept, uphold, and recite it to seek the removal of obstacles and the increase of merit.
*The Heart Sūtra Explained as Clearly as One’s Palm* (End).
